Projects Spring 2021 – Fall 2023 Roslindale, Boston, MA

From four vacant lots to a growing community

How a five-person steering committee turned neglected city lots into a thriving garden network — raising $85,000, signing on three nonprofit partners, and connecting 120 families to growing plots over two years. No staff, no office, no prior grant experience.

4 Community gardens established
120 Families with garden plots
$85K Raised in grants & donations
3 Nonprofit partnerships formed

Background: A Neighborhood in Transition

Roslindale is a dense, diverse neighborhood in southwest Boston — part triple-decker residential streets, part neighborhood commercial squares. In 2020, like many urban neighborhoods, it was navigating the overlapping strains of a pandemic, housing pressure, and an intensifying conversation about food access and green space that the pandemic had accelerated.

Within a six-block radius of Roslindale Square, four parcels of city-owned land sat empty. A former commercial building site, two lots from a mid-2000s redevelopment project that stalled, and one corner property that had been vacant for more than a decade. The lots weren't eyesores — the city kept them mowed — but they were doing nothing for anyone.

Maya Chen, a nurse and longtime Roslindale resident, had been growing vegetables in five-gallon buckets on her apartment deck for three years. She wasn't alone. At the height of the pandemic, she started noticing neighbors posting about container gardens, window boxes, and backyard plots in the neighborhood Facebook group. She started asking a question: what would it take to turn those empty lots into gardens?

The Problem Was Bigger Than It Looked

What started as an informal question became a structured project when Maya teamed up with Roberto Santos, a former city planner who'd moved to the neighborhood in 2019, and three other neighbors — a retired teacher, a small business owner, and a youth organizer from a local high school.

Their initial research surfaced more than just an appetite for gardens. According to the Greater Boston Food Bank's regional hunger survey, 18% of households in Roslindale's primary ZIP code reported experiencing food insecurity in 2020 — up from 11% in 2018. The neighborhood had one full-service grocery store, served a population of approximately 35,000 residents, and had a substantial percentage of residents with no car access.

But the group also knew that food access alone doesn't explain why a community garden takes hold. They'd visited successful projects in Jamaica Plain and Hyde Park. The ones that worked weren't just about growing food — they were about space. A place to be outside, to know your neighbors, to have something that was yours in a neighborhood where most people rent.

"We didn't start by applying for grants. We started by walking around the neighborhood for two months, knocking on doors and asking people what they actually wanted. That's what made everything else possible."

Maya Chen, Project Lead, Roslindale Community Garden Network

Phase 1: Outreach Before Anything Else

Before approaching the city, before writing a grant, before designing a garden layout, the steering committee ran a structured outreach campaign across three weekends in the spring of 2021. Using an early version of what became Civic Signal's Community Outreach Checklist, they organized 18 volunteers into canvassing pairs and covered 340 households in the target area.

The results were clear: 78% of respondents expressed interest in a garden plot if one were available; 62% said they'd be willing to volunteer at least twice per year; 43% said access to fresh vegetables was a real concern for their household. And perhaps most importantly for the grant process that would follow: 91% said they'd heard about at least one of the four vacant lots and had wondered what might be done with them.

Outreach data as grant evidence

The community survey results became the centerpiece of every grant proposal the group submitted. Roberto Santos, who wrote most of the proposals, says the 78% interest figure was cited in two of their three successful grant applications as the primary evidence of community need.

The outreach also produced something less quantifiable: a list of 47 people who had asked to stay involved. That list became the steering committee's primary communication list throughout the project — and several members of that group became the first garden plot holders in 2022.

Phase 2: Monthly Meetings, One Decision at a Time

Starting in June 2021, the steering committee held monthly public meetings — always at 6:30 PM on a weeknight, always in the same room at the Roslindale branch library, always using a structured agenda. The consistency was deliberate.

Roberto Santos adapted a version of Civic Signal's Public Meeting Agenda Template for each meeting, adding specific action items from the previous month and a standing "community announcements" section that often ran five to ten minutes over but kept people feeling connected to what was happening. Attendance ranged from 12 to 46 people — with the higher numbers on nights when the group had a specific decision to make.

Key decisions made through this process included: the naming of the project ("Roslindale Community Garden Network"), the governance structure (a nine-person board with elected plot-holder representation), the plot assignment lottery system, rules around composting and water use, and the terms of the partnership agreements with the three nonprofit partners.

"We could have decided all of that in a back room in a weekend. But we didn't, and I think that's why it worked. People felt like it was theirs because they were in the room when the decisions happened."

Roberto Santos, Grant Writer & Co-Founder, RCGN

Phase 3: The Funding Strategy

The group's funding strategy followed the framework now documented in Civic Signal's Grant Readiness Guide — though Roberto had arrived at a similar approach through intuition and advice from a more experienced grant writer at a peer organization.

Before applying anywhere, they secured fiscal sponsorship through Roslindale Square Main Streets, an existing 501(c)(3) commercial district organization that agreed to administer grants on their behalf while they built toward independent nonprofit status. That relationship, brokered through a board member of Main Streets who also attended the community meetings, opened doors that would have been closed to a brand-new volunteer group.

The Funder Sequence

Rather than applying to everyone at once, the group identified three tiers of funders and worked sequentially:

  1. Local first — a $12,000 seed grant from the Boston Parks Foundation, secured in fall 2021, before the first lot was even cleared. This grant funded soil testing, materials for two raised beds, and a part-time project coordinator at 10 hours/week.
  2. Regional second — Two grants from regional foundations totaling $38,000, applied for in early 2022 after the first two gardens were operational and they had photo documentation, plot-holder testimonials, and clear outcomes to report.
  3. Neighborhood donors third — A neighborhood fundraising campaign in fall 2022, anchored by a harvest dinner at the largest garden site, raised $14,000 from individual donors and a local restaurant that provided the food at cost. The city council member for the district matched the first $5,000.

The remaining $21,000 came from a CDBG sub-grant through the city, awarded in 2023 after the project had two full years of documentation behind it.

Project Timeline

March 2021
Project Begins
Maya Chen convenes five neighbors for an initial planning conversation. The group agrees on a structure: a volunteer steering committee with no staff, meeting monthly.
April–May 2021
Community Outreach Campaign
Three weekend canvassing events cover 340 households. 47 residents express strong interest in getting involved. Survey data becomes the foundation of the group's grant strategy.
June 2021
First Public Meeting
28 people attend the first monthly meeting at the Roslindale library. The group votes to name the project and form a formal steering committee. Roberto Santos joins as grant writer.
September 2021
First Grant Awarded — $12,000
Boston Parks Foundation awards a $12,000 seed grant. The group uses it for soil testing, initial raised beds, and a part-time coordinator. Fiscal sponsorship through Roslindale Square Main Streets is confirmed.
Winter 2021–2022
Lot Access Negotiations
After six months of back-and-forth with the city's Parks & Recreation department, the group secures 5-year use agreements for all four lots. The agreements include liability coverage through the city's policy.
May 2022
First Gardens Open
Two of the four garden sites open with 40 raised beds each. A lottery assigns 80 plots to community members, prioritizing residents of nearby buildings. A third partner organization, Urban Sprouts, agrees to run gardening workshops monthly.
Summer–Fall 2022
Regional Grants Awarded — $38,000
Two regional foundation grants totaling $38,000 arrive, based largely on documented outcomes from the first growing season: 80 active plot-holders, 12 community workshops, and a documented produce harvest shared with a local food pantry.
October 2022
Harvest Dinner Fundraiser — $14,000
A harvest dinner attended by 120 people raises $14,000 in individual donations and a matched gift from the district city councilor. The event becomes an annual tradition.
Spring 2023
Two Additional Gardens Open
The remaining two lots open. Total plot capacity reaches 200, with 120 actively assigned to families. A waitlist of 60 households forms — fueling advocacy for two more sites currently under negotiation.
Fall 2023
CDBG Grant Awarded — $21,000
A CDBG sub-grant through the city funds a second project coordinator position, expanded composting infrastructure, and an accessibility audit resulting in 12 raised beds designed for wheelchair access.

Outcomes

4 Community gardens across Roslindale
120 Active family garden plots
$85K Total raised in 2.5 years
3 Nonprofit partnerships signed
200+ Volunteer hours per season
60 Households on the waitlist

Partnership Organizations

Roslindale Square Main Streets
Fiscal Sponsor

Commercial district organization that served as fiscal sponsor from fall 2021 through 2023, while RCGN pursued its own 501(c)(3) status. The relationship was brokered through a shared board member and required no formal payment — Main Streets considered the partnership a community benefit aligned with their mission.

Urban Sprouts
Programming Partner

Boston-based urban agriculture organization that provided monthly gardening workshops at all four sites and connected plot-holders to seed libraries and composting resources. The partnership reduced the need for RCGN to develop in-house programming expertise.

Roslindale Community Food Pantry
Food Access Partner

Arrangement whereby plot-holders can donate surplus produce directly to the food pantry through a weekly drop point installed at the largest garden site. In 2023, garden members donated an estimated 800 pounds of fresh vegetables through this program.

Five Lessons from the Field

Lesson 01
Outreach data is not optional

The 78% interest rate from the community survey didn't just make the grant application stronger — it gave the steering committee the confidence to keep going when the city negotiations stalled. When you've documented that your neighbors want something, "this is hard" stops being a reason to quit.

Lesson 02
The meeting IS the organizing

Every decision made at the monthly public meetings was harder to make than if five people had made it in a living room. But every decision also stuck. There was no one who could come back six months later and say "I didn't know about that" — because the decision had been made in a room where they could have been. Public process is slow and it's worth it.

Lesson 03
Fiscal sponsorship unlocks your first year

Don't wait for 501(c)(3) status before you start fundraising. Find a fiscal sponsor — ideally an organization that shares your values and community — and use their structure while you build yours. The year RCGN spent under Main Streets' umbrella was the year they built the track record that made independent funding possible.

Lesson 04
Sequence your funders

The steering committee resisted the urge to apply to everyone at once. They built documentation at every stage — photos, attendance sheets, testimonials, harvest tallies — and brought increasingly strong evidence to each successive funder. By the time they applied for the CDBG grant, they had two years of proof behind them. This is the opposite of how most volunteer groups approach grant-seeking.

Lesson 05
The waitlist is your advocacy tool

Sixty households on a waitlist is not a failure — it's evidence of demand that justifies the next phase of expansion. RCGN is currently using the waitlist data in conversations with the city about two additional sites. The list didn't exist because they hadn't served everyone; it existed because the community need was larger than their first-phase capacity. That's a story worth telling.
